### Library entrance closure: Monday to Thursday

The library will remain open on its usual schedule while the pavement outside the east entrance is replaced from Monday through Thursday. The east entrance, which faces the bus shelter, will be closed to everyone during the work. Please use the west entrance, which faces the playground.

If you are coming from the playground, you can use the west entrance as normal. If you are coming from the bus shelter, follow the signed path along the south side of the building to the west entrance. This route adds approximately 120 metres to your journey. It has no steps, but one section has a temporary firm mat over uneven ground. The mat is on the route to the west entrance; the east entrance remains closed, including to wheelchair users. The bus shelter will remain available, but the direct path from it to the east entrance will be behind a temporary barrier.

During library opening hours, staff can meet visitors at the bus shelter and accompany them to the west entrance. If you would like this assistance, call the library desk before setting out. You can also request assistance on arrival by calling the number displayed at the shelter, but a staff member may not be available immediately. The library cannot provide transport around the building.

The returns slot beside the east entrance will also be inaccessible. Books due Monday through Thursday may be returned on Friday without a late charge, including books borrowed from another branch.

Heavy rain may delay the work. If the closure is extended, an updated notice will be posted at both entrances and at the bus shelter. The Friday return arrangement will remain in place unless the updated notice announces a further extension.

Welcome to the garden! Your assigned bed has the same number as your membership card. Some painted numbers have faded, so check the plan on the noticeboard if you are unsure. Please ask a steward before planting in a bed whose number you cannot read. The narrow strip beside the compost bins is planted collectively; it is not an unclaimed bed.

Tools with blue handles are shared. Please return them to the shed before you leave, even if you plan to come back later that evening. Tools without blue handles may belong to another gardener, so do not assume they are shared. You will find the shed code on your membership card. Please close the door when you leave to keep rain off the lower shelves.

The watering rota covers the collective strip and the young fruit trees, but not individual beds—even those belonging to gardeners on the rota. If you will be away, you can arrange separately for another gardener to water your bed. Only add the arrangement to the noticeboard once they have agreed, so a request does not look like a job someone has accepted.

Weeds without seed heads can go into the green compost bay. Put weeds with seed heads into the covered brown bin. If you are unsure whether a plant has set seed, put it in the brown bin and ask at the next steward session. This is simply a sorting precaution, not a judgment about anyone’s gardening.

Stewards are usually here on Saturday mornings. Check the noticeboard for the next session and any cancellation. We are glad you are here, and we would always rather answer a small question before planting than help move a thriving crop out of somebody else’s bed.

We compared two worksheets for subtracting background from fluorescence measurements. The current worksheet requires an operator to enter a blank reading separately for each sample; the proposed worksheet imports the blank reading from the instrument log to reduce transcription. The comparison assessed agreement between corrected values and the time required to produce them. It did not assess accuracy relative to a known true concentration, and no certified reference material was included.

Twenty-four aliquots from eight prepared solutions, with three aliquots per solution, were measured in one session in a fixed order by solution number. Both worksheets processed the same instrument readings; each aliquot was measured only once. The operator completed the manual worksheet before the imported worksheet was generated and could not see the imported results during manual entry. Although each solution contributed multiple aliquots, the worksheet comparison did not include independent repeat measurements of each aliquot’s instrument signal.

In the initial comparison, corrected values agreed at the instrument’s displayed precision for 21 of the 24 aliquots. All three differences occurred in the final solution, where a single blank entry had been copied into three rows of the manual worksheet. Inspection of the saved instrument log showed that this entry was 0.2 fluorescence units higher than the blank assigned to those rows in the log, making the manual corrected values 0.2 units lower. In a separate correction performed after the initial comparison, replacing the copied entry with the logged blank brought all 24 corrected values into agreement at the displayed precision.

The initial discrepancies are consistent with a transcription error propagated across three rows, rather than three independent transcription errors. They cannot be used to estimate a routine operator error rate: only one operator participated, and that operator knew the comparison concerned data entry. Agreement after correction supports the conclusion that the import applied the intended subtraction to these inputs. It does not establish agreement beyond the displayed precision, accuracy relative to true concentration, or correct blank assignment in future instrument logs.

The imported worksheet took four minutes to produce, compared with eleven minutes for manual entry and checking—a seven-minute reduction in this session. These timings excluded instrument operation and the subsequent discrepancy investigation. The observed reduction applies to this session and its particular number of rows; whether it persists when log formats change or an operator must resolve a missing blank was not assessed.

Returning keyboard focus to a cell puts the cursor back. Does it put the user back in context? This hypothetical study asked whether speaking the current row label after a note closes helps screen-reader users return to a table.

Twelve experienced screen-reader users completed four tasks with each of two versions. One spoke the row label when the note closed. The existing version returned focus to the same cell without the added cue. Six participants used the cue version first; six used the existing version first. The two task sets used different tables, and table assignments were reversed for half of each order group.

We timed the interval from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Reading the note was outside that interval. We calculated each participant’s mean completion time for each version, then took the median of those twelve means. That median was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. The three-second gap is a difference between two medians, not the median of twelve within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower personal mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means at the recorded precision. We have not calculated a confidence interval or performed a significance test. These descriptive results do not establish a reliable speed benefit.

Did the cue help people feel oriented? Nine participants said it did in the closing interview. Four of those nine also described occasions when it interrupted speech they were still listening to. The same cue could help with orientation and interfere with listening. These reports describe participants’ experience; they are not a measured improvement in search performance.

The other three participants did not report an orientation benefit. None asked for the feature to be removed from the prototype, but that does not tell us whether they wanted it enabled by default. We did not ask participants to choose a default.

The ordering scheme reduced the alignment between version and practice without removing every possible learning effect. A search strategy learned in the first task set may have carried into the second. The study also leaves two scope questions open: how less experienced users would respond, and how the cue would work in large tables. All participants were experienced, and the prototype tables fit within one screen.

For the product team, an orientation benefit is plausible for some users under these tasks. Added speech can also compete with ongoing speech. That competition needs attention even if a time difference eventually proves reliable. A next version could make the cue interruptible, then test whether users can get the location information without losing speech they still need. We did not implement or test that behavior here. The present timings cannot serve as evidence for it.

The waiting list has grown, and the proposed answer is to divide every returning gardener’s bed in half. I understand the appeal: there are twenty full beds and ten households waiting, and access to shared land should not depend on having joined years ago. But fairness involves more than the size of each plot. It also involves how we move from one allocation to another, including whether gardeners can keep established crops through their growing cycles. For that reason, I support dividing vacant beds first and allowing returning gardeners to keep their present beds for one more season.

Four full beds will become vacant at the end of this season. Dividing them would create eight half beds for the coming season. If every offer is accepted, eight households would receive beds and two would remain waiting. That is a real shortfall, not a cleared waiting list. The proposal would nevertheless open places for most households now waiting without requiring every returning gardener to remove established planting at once.

The strongest objection is that protecting established planting may also protect an established advantage. Sometimes it does. Planting a perennial cannot give someone a permanent claim to shared land, and our membership agreement promises a bed for one season, with renewal decided annually. The justification for this proposal is therefore a limited transition, not an entitlement to continued occupancy. Returning gardeners would keep their current beds for one more season, and the committee would publish the following season’s allocation rule before renewals open.

That advance notice must apply to new members as well. A household accepting a half bed needs to know the rules governing its future, just as a returning gardener does. If new members learn only afterward that their beds will be merged or moved, we will have reproduced the same uncertainty on smaller plots. The published rule should cover both groups. I do not yet have a preferred permanent bed size; we can decide how to manage this transition without claiming to have settled the permanent allocation.

The raised beds also require separate consideration. Two of the twenty full beds are reserved for gardeners who need them, and neither is among the four becoming vacant. My proposal preserves that reservation and the existing access assessment. Equal area does not necessarily mean equal access: a standard half bed is not automatically a substitute for a raised bed.

Location presents a further limitation. All four vacancies are at the far end of the site, so all eight new households would begin in the same area. Voluntary exchanges with returning members could help, but they cannot be counted as a guaranteed part of the proposal. Nor should a household have to negotiate a private favor to obtain a usable route to its bed. Before making offers, the committee should check the paths to the new half beds and report any access problem it cannot resolve.

Offers would follow the waiting list’s current order. This preserves whatever disadvantages households faced in learning about the list, and that concern deserves attention. But changing the order during this allocation would introduce another contested decision without advance notice to those affected. We should begin reviewing how the list is advertised now and announce any future change in ordering before it applies.

The choice before the meeting is therefore between transitions with different costs. Dividing vacant beds first would leave two households waiting if all eight offers are accepted. Dividing occupied beds immediately might create more places, while spreading disruption across more gardeners and established crops. I support the vacancy-first transition because it expands access substantially while limiting immediate disruption and requiring advance notice of the next allocation rule. That judgment does not erase the cost to those still waiting. The meeting should weigh that cost alongside the disruption of immediate division, with neither left out of the decision.

That rule should cover both returning and new members. A household accepting a half bed also needs to know whether beds will later be merged or moved. Otherwise, we risk passing the same uncertainty on to new gardeners. I do not yet favor a particular permanent bed size. We can agree on this transition while leaving that question open, provided we set a clear deadline for the next allocation rule.

Access needs must remain part of the allocation decision. Two of the twenty full beds are raised beds reserved for gardeners who need them, and neither is among the four becoming vacant. My proposal keeps that reservation and the existing access assessment unchanged. A standard half bed is not automatically a substitute for a raised bed, even if both are counted by area on the plan.

Starting with vacancies also has a practical drawback: all four are at the far end of the site, so all eight new households would begin in the same area. We could invite returning members to exchange locations voluntarily, but we cannot count on those exchanges. Nor should a new household have to negotiate a private favor to get a usable route to its bed. Before making offers, the committee should check the paths to the new half beds and report any access problem it cannot resolve.

For these offers, the waiting list would retain its current order. This preserves whatever disadvantages households faced in learning about the list, and that deserves attention. I would like the next set of fraction worksheets to include one worked example followed by a problem that asks pupils to explain a different method. Our current sheets give a sequence of steps and then ask pupils to repeat it. This is useful when the immediate aim is to practise the sequence. I am less sure that successful repetition tells us whether pupils understand why it applies.

Last week’s lesson brought that distinction into focus. After copying an example with equal denominators, several pupils added the numerators and denominators separately on a later question. I had not collected a starting question, so I do not know how many already held that misunderstanding. Nor can I say that the worked example caused it; it may simply have exposed it. What I can say is that correct copying on the first practice question did not prevent the misunderstanding from appearing on the next.

The proposed explanation problem would show two correct solutions to the same fraction addition: one using equivalent fractions and one using a diagram. Pupils would explain where the same quantity appears in both solutions. This would give us something beyond repeated steps to consider when judging their understanding. It would not ask which method is always better. A diagram may clarify these numbers but become cumbersome with others, and I would not want a useful representation to become another compulsory routine.

The change would take space and lesson time, so I would replace one repetition question rather than add another page. Pupils who need more practice with the original sequence could use the spare practice sheet we already have. That is a practical arrangement, not evidence that one explanation problem will meet everyone’s needs.

We could try the revised sheet in one lesson and collect pupils’ explanations before deciding whether to keep it. This would help us see what the responses reveal about pupils’ understanding and whether teachers find the change workable. Without a comparison planned in advance, it would not establish that the revised sheet improves attainment. I think the opportunity to learn those more limited things is enough reason to try a bounded change.

**Claim.** Let \((a_n)_{n\ge1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing real sequence with limit zero, and put
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then each \(d_n\ge0\), and
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1.
\]
For every integer \(N\ge1\), the tail after \(N\) terms is
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, this tail is less than any prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) when \(N\) is sufficiently large.

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\ge a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\ge0\).

To find the sum of the series, first consider its partial sum:
\[
S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1}).
\]
Every intermediate term cancels, leaving
\[
S_N=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\]
Thus
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Because \(a_{N+1}\) tends to zero, the partial sums \(S_N\) approach \(a_1\). By definition, this means that the series converges to \(a_1\).

Now fix \(N\ge1\). For any integer \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})
=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\]
The difference between this finite tail sum and \(a_{N+1}\) has absolute value \(a_{M+1}\), which tends to zero as \(M\) increases. Hence the infinite tail converges and equals
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]

Finally, let \(\varepsilon>0\). Since \(a_n\to0\), there is an integer \(K\ge1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) for every \(k\ge K\). For every \(N\ge K\), we therefore have
\[
0\le\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]

No strict decrease is needed: equal consecutive terms simply give \(d_n=0\). If \(a_1=0\), nonnegativity and monotonicity force every \(a_n=0\), and all the identities still hold. \(\square\)

**Claim.** Let \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing real sequence with limit zero, and put
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then every \(d_n\) is nonnegative,
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1,
\]
and, for every integer \(N\geq 1\),
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an \(N\geq 1\) such that the tail after \(N\) terms is less than \(\varepsilon\).

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\geq a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\geq 0\).

To find the sum of the series, we first compute its partial sum:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_N
&=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n\\
&=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\
&=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each intermediate term cancels, leaving only the first and last terms. Thus
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Because \(a_n\to 0\), this difference tends to zero. More explicitly, given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose an integer \(K\geq 1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) whenever \(k\geq K\). Then, for every \(N\geq K\),
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
The partial sums therefore converge to \(a_1\), which is what it means for the series to converge to \(a_1\).

Now fix \(N\geq 1\). For every integer \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
&=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The difference between this finite sum and \(a_{N+1}\) is
\[
\left|\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n-a_{N+1}\right|
=a_{M+1}\longrightarrow 0.
\]
Thus the tail series converges, and its sum is exactly \(a_{N+1}\). With \(K\) chosen as above, taking \(N=K\) gives
\[

**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) be the number of ways to select \(k\) plots so that no two neighboring plots are selected, including the two plots at the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** When \(k=0\), the only selection is the empty selection, and the formula gives
\[
\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1.
\]

Now suppose \(k\ge1\). Count pairs consisting of a valid selection and one of its selected plots marked as the start. Each selection gives \(k\) such pairs, so there are \(kA(n,k)\) pairs.

To count the same pairs another way, choose the start plot in \(n\) ways. Starting there and moving clockwise, let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot, for \(i=1,\ldots,k\). If \(k=1\), this gap consists of all the other plots before returning to the start. Each \(g_i\) is positive because neighboring plots cannot both be selected, and the gaps contain all \(n-k\) unselected plots. Thus
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k.
\]

The number of ordered lists of \(k\) positive integers with this sum is \(\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\): represent \(n-k\) as a row of objects and choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) spaces between them as separators. The resulting \(k\) groups give the gap sizes. Each start plot and gap list determines exactly one marked selection, including when the gaps are all one. Hence
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1},
\qquad
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

Expanding the factorials gives
\[
\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
=\frac{n}{k}\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]
The division by \(k\) is legitimate because each valid selection has exactly \(k\) possible choices of the marked plot. The plots have fixed labels, so rotations are not identified. \(\square\)

**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) distinctly labeled garden plots in a circle. For \(0\le k\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) count the \(k\)-element selections with no neighboring plots selected, including neighbors across the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** If \(k=0\), there is exactly one selection: the empty selection. The formula also gives \(1\), since
\[
\frac{n}{n}\binom n0=1.
\]

Now assume \(k\ge1\). Count valid selections with one selected plot marked as the start. Each valid selection has exactly \(k\) choices for this mark, so there are \(kA(n,k)\) marked selections.

We can also construct a marked selection by first choosing its start plot, in \(n\) ways. Beginning there, number the selected plots clockwise. Let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot, with the last gap returning to the start. When \(k=1\), this single gap contains all \(n-1\) other plots.

The no-neighbors condition says that every \(g_i\) is positive. Since the gaps contain all the unselected plots exactly once,
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k.
\]
To count these ordered gap lists, put \(n-k\) objects in a row and choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) internal spaces for separators. The resulting \(k\) nonempty groups have sizes \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\), and every positive gap list arises uniquely this way. Thus there are
\[
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
\]
gap lists. For \(k=1\), choosing no separators gives the single required gap.

A start plot and a gap list determine a unique marked selection: move clockwise, leaving \(g_i\) unselected plots after each selected plot before reaching the next. The \(k\) selected plots and the \(n-k\) gap plots fill exactly one circuit, so the last gap closes at the start. Conversely, reading the gaps of a marked selection recovers that start and list. Therefore
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]
Dividing by \(k\) is legitimate because each unmarked selection was counted exactly \(k\) times, once for each selected plot that could be marked. Hence
\[
A(n,k)=\frac nk\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
=\frac nk\frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), all gaps equal \(1\), which the construction allows. No division by rotations is needed: the labels occupy fixed positions, and choosing a different start is precisely the marking already accounted for. \(\square\)

**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) be the number of \(k\)-element selections with no two neighboring plots selected, including the pair across the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** If \(k=0\), there is exactly one selection, the empty selection. The formula also gives
\[
\frac{n}{n}\binom{n}{0}=1.
\]

Now suppose \(k\ge 1\). We count valid selections with one selected plot marked as the start. Every valid selection has exactly \(k\) choices for its marked plot, so the number of marked selections is
\[
kA(n,k).
\]

We can also construct a marked selection by choosing its start and specifying the gaps between consecutive selected plots. There are \(n\) choices for the start. Beginning there, number the selected plots \(1,\ldots,k\) in clockwise order, and let \(g_i\) count the unselected plots after selected plot \(i\) and before the next selected plot. The last gap returns to the start, so it checks adjacency across the circular boundary as well. When \(k=1\), this single gap contains all \(n-1\) other plots.

No two selected plots are neighbors precisely when every gap is positive. Since there are \(n-k\) unselected plots altogether, we need
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k,
\qquad g_i\ge 1.
\]

To count these ordered gap tuples, place \(n-k\) objects in a row. Choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) internal spaces for separators. The resulting \(k\) nonempty groups have sizes \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\). Conversely, each positive gap tuple determines exactly those separator positions. Thus there are
\[
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
\]
gap tuples. For \(k=1\), we choose no separators and obtain the single group of size \(n-1\).

A start and a gap tuple determine exactly one marked selection: move clockwise from the start, leaving \(g_i\) unselected plots before placing the next selected plot. Because
\[
k+\sum_{i=1}^k g_i=n,
\]
this construction goes exactly once around the circle and returns to the start. Recovering the start and gaps from the marked selection reverses the construction. Therefore,
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

Dividing by \(k\) is legitimate because each unmarked selection was counted exactly once for each of its \(k\) selected plots. Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(n,k)
&=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\\
&=\frac{n(n-k-1)!}{k!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap is one, which the construction allows. We do not divide by rotations: the plots have fixed, distinct labels, so selections using different labels are different selections. \(\square\)

The compost thermometer has returned from its brief career as a dibber. It is back on the hook inside the shed, where it can resume measuring temperature rather than making holes. Please use the wooden dibbers for planting. They have fewer opinions about heat.

This month we are comparing the middle of the active heap with its outer edge. On your rota day, take one reading at each marked position and record both on the sheet. Push the probe to the mark on its shaft, wait until the display settles, and wipe the probe before returning the thermometer to the hook. If the display never settles, write that down instead of choosing the number you like best.

A warmer middle is interesting, but a single pair of readings will not tell us whether the whole heap is ready to use. We are collecting observations over the month. The stewards will also inspect the material before deciding whether to open the bay for collection. Until the notice changes, please keep adding suitable material to the active bay and leave the resting bay alone.

The recording sheet has room for comments because weather, recently added material, and an uncooperative display may help explain a reading. You do not need to write a small novel. “Heavy rain this morning” is useful. “The heap has entered a troubled period” is less useful, though we appreciate the concern.

The balance readings were stable during the twenty-minute observation period. Stability here means that the displayed mass stayed within 0.01 grams of its initial displayed value. It does not mean that the initial value was accurate. We did not place a certified reference mass on the balance during this check.

The same sealed container remained on the pan throughout. This avoids variability from replacing the container, but it also means that the check says nothing about repeatability after unloading and reloading. The maintenance record should preserve that distinction.

The room temperature recorded at the start and end was the same to the wall sensor's displayed precision. There were no readings between those times. We therefore cannot exclude a temporary temperature change during the observation period, nor can we determine whether such a change would have affected this balance. The temperature record is context for the check, not a correction applied to the mass readings.

No visible condensation appeared on the container. That observation does not measure moisture exchange, because the check included neither a humidity measurement nor an independent mass reference. We report it to describe what the operator saw, not to establish a mechanism for the stable display.

These results support a narrow entry in the maintenance log: no displayed drift beyond the stated tolerance during this placement and observation period. A calibration decision would require the separate reference-mass procedure.

To request material for that day’s retrieval, submit your request before noon and include the item’s shelfmark. These requests will be collected together for retrieval at 2 p.m. There will be no second afternoon retrieval during the trial.

Your request must arrive before noon; you do not need to arrive before noon yourself. If you have requested a map in advance, you can arrive later. If you arrive later without having made a request, you can still use the catalogues and open shelves and submit a request for the next opening day.

Requests without a shelfmark will be held while staff help identify the item. Once identified, the item will join the next retrieval, which may not be on the day the request was first received.

Maps identified as fragile require a support prepared by the conservation team. We will count delayed requests and review reader comments before deciding whether to continue the arrangement. A comment card will be available at the desk throughout the six-week trial.

Rain can alter acoustic recordings as well as animal calling, complicating comparisons between wet and dry surveys. This pilot examined whether a rain shield changed the output of a fixed call detector. It did not estimate animal abundance; calling activity itself is an ecological outcome only when it matches the question being asked.

We placed two recorders in each of twelve habitat patches, with shielded and exposed positions assigned by coin toss within each patch. The recorders operated simultaneously. We analyzed twelve paired ten-minute windows per patch, yielding 144 paired windows: 48 classified as wet and 96 as dry from field logs. Weather was observed, not assigned. A window was positive if the detector marked at least one target call, using the same detector settings throughout.

During wet windows, the recorders agreed in 29 of 48 pairs; twelve pairs were positive only on the shielded recorder and seven only on the exposed recorder. During dry windows, they agreed in 84 of 96 pairs, with five shield-only and seven exposed-only positives. Agreement includes both jointly positive and jointly negative pairs, which were not separated in this summary. The agreement counts therefore cannot be interpreted as the number of windows containing calls.

The excess of shield-only over exposed-only positives during wet windows is consistent with shielding changing detector output under rain. The direction of discordance was reversed during dry windows. These descriptive patterns do not establish that shielding recovered genuine calls: without independent call labels, we cannot determine whether discordant detections reflect true calls or detector errors. Nor do the results establish that rain reduced calling. Weather was not experimentally assigned, and repeated windows within patches mean that the 144 paired windows are not 144 independent ecological replicates.

The paired comparison identifies a measurement issue to resolve before using these recordings to infer ecological trends. A future study could include blinded human labeling to assess detection validity and more patches to broaden replication. For now, the data describe disagreement between shielded and exposed recordings within the observed weather categories, while leaving its biological interpretation open.

The persistence rule was motivated by the concern that a single pressure spike need not indicate a valve fault. It requires two threshold crossings within a cycle before raising an alarm, whereas the comparison rule uses a higher threshold and alarms after one crossing. Both thresholds and the persistence requirement were fixed using a separate setup recording; the evaluation recordings were not used to select them. Because the persistence rule also uses a lower threshold, the comparison evaluates two fixed rules rather than isolating the effect of persistence.

The held-out bench set comprised 120 machine cycles from one machine: 30 with an induced valve fault and 90 with no induced fault. Each rule produced at most one alarm per cycle. The persistence rule alarmed in 24 of the 30 fault cycles and eight of the 90 no-fault cycles; the comparison rule alarmed in 21 fault cycles and three no-fault cycles. Thus, the persistence rule detected more induced faults but also alarmed more often in cycles designated no-fault. This designation means only that no fault was induced: the machine was not dismantled after every cycle to exclude all possible defects.

Eighteen fault cycles triggered both rules. Within this shared subset, the mean time from logged fault onset to the first alarm was 2.1 seconds for the persistence rule and 2.8 seconds for the comparison rule. Comparing delays on the same cycles avoids differences arising from the composition of the detected sets. However, it excludes faults detected by only one rule and faults missed by both, so the delay result applies only to shared detections.

The observed benefit therefore differs from the rule’s motivation. Although persistence was introduced to address transient spikes, this experiment showed higher detection of induced faults at the cost of more alarms in no-fault cycles. Neither the rule’s construction nor these results establish better false-alarm control.

These recordings evaluate two fixed rules under one bench arrangement. They do not establish performance on a production line or with naturally developing faults. No preferred rule was selected because that choice depends on the relative costs of missing a fault and interrupting a cycle, neither of which was measured.

The committee should choose the handling replica for the navigation exhibit this season because it better fits the exhibit’s current question: how does a reading change when an instrument is tilted? Visitors cannot tilt the original. The replica would let them investigate that question directly, although whether the proposed activity helps them understand it remains to be tested.

The original’s availability on loan is a real opportunity, and one that may not recur. It offers something the replica cannot: a material connection to the instrument’s working history. A maker’s correction remains visible on its scale, providing a basis for an account of repair and adaptation. A photograph would not give every visitor the same experience as standing beside the object. These strengths support considering the original, but they do not establish that it best serves the exhibit we have designed. Our current text concerns reading and error. Making repair central would require a change in direction and a different use of the season’s remaining preparation time.

Cost supports the choice of the replica without deciding it. The loan would cost 18,000 units from the exhibit budget, including transport, insurance, and a sealed case. The replica would cost 7,000 units, including replacement parts for the season. Both fit the allocated budget, and neither quote is a complete estimate of staff time. The reason to prefer the replica is therefore what visitors would be permitted to do, not that the loan is unaffordable. Its lower quoted cost would also leave more resources available for testing the activity.

That testing is necessary. The replica’s moving parts could distract visitors from the question, or visitors could turn them without noticing the scale. A visitor trial has not yet happened, so we should not claim that handling has already improved understanding. The recommendation rests on the replica’s fit with the intended activity, not on a demonstrated teaching benefit.

Choosing the replica now would preserve the exhibit’s focus while leaving resources to test how well the activity works. We should retain a clearly labeled photograph of the original and explain why the replica can be handled. If the committee instead wants the original’s history to become the central question, it should explicitly authorize that change in the exhibit’s direction.

We propose revising the short discovery labels attached to twenty digitized collections. Some labels repeat terms from old inventory headings without explaining whose categories they were. The scanned inventories would remain available exactly as they are. This distinction matters: changing the archive’s present description of a collection is different from changing the historical document. Yet discovery labels are also part of how the archive represents its collections. Revising them therefore requires justification, even when the source documents remain untouched.

The case for revision begins with two ways readers reach the material. A reader following a quotation from an inventory benefits from finding the same words in the catalogue. The existing labels provide that consistency, and its value for retrieval should be preserved. A reader who has not seen the inventory, however, may reasonably understand the label as the archive’s present description. Repeating an old heading without context can thus help one reader find a collection while misleading another about how the archive describes it. Both needs deserve attention.

We propose using a current descriptive label, adding a note identifying the original heading, and retaining that heading as a searchable alternative. The historical words would remain a route into the collection without standing alone as its present description. Search results would display the current label; the note would be visible when a reader opened the catalogue record. Neither the words in the historical document nor access to the old inventory would change.

A reasonable objection is that a replacement label interprets the collection. It does. But selecting an inventory heading as the main discovery label also interprets the collection, even when that selection appears simply to copy the source. The question is therefore how well the label describes the material and how clearly it shows its relationship to the historical wording. A new label should describe the contents at the level the collection supports, and the accompanying note should make that relationship visible. This standard does not establish that our drafts meet it: labels have been drafted for all twenty collections, but readers and subject specialists have not yet reviewed them.

There is also a practical objection: contextual notes can make a short catalogue harder to scan. Keeping the note inside the record preserves brevity in search results, but it means a reader may not immediately see the historical wording. Retaining that wording as searchable helps preserve retrieval from quotations; it does not eliminate the tradeoff over what readers see first.

These limits support a trial rather than wider adoption. We recommend testing the proposal with the twenty collections, followed by checks of both successful and failed searches. We have no evidence yet that it will improve retrieval. The trial would test whether this approach can provide context while preserving a route from historical quotations. Expanding the policy before that check would go beyond what the present case supports.

Its purpose is to test whether this approach can provide context while preserving a route from historical quotations. The present case does not support expanding the policy before those checks.

**Proposition.** Let \(A\ge 0\), let \(c_0\in\mathbb R\), and suppose the real corrections \(\delta_k\) satisfy
\[
|\delta_k|\le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)}
\qquad(k\ge 0).
\]
Define the cumulative corrected values by
\[
c_n=c_0+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\delta_k
\qquad(n\ge 0),
\]
where the sum is empty when \(n=0\). Then \(c_n\) converges to a finite real limit \(c\), and
\[
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}
\qquad(m\ge 0).
\]

**Proof.** For integers \(n>m\ge 0\), the difference \(c_n-c_m\) is the sum of the corrections applied from index \(m\) through index \(n-1\). By the triangle inequality,
\[
|c_n-c_m|
\le \sum_{k=m}^{n-1}|\delta_k|
\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}.
\]
The identity
\[
\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}
=\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}
\]
makes this last sum telescope. Consequently,
\[
|c_n-c_m|
\le A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)
\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
\tag{1}
\]

This estimate shows that sufficiently late cumulative values are arbitrarily close to one another. Indeed, given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose an integer \(M\ge 0\) such that \(A/(M+1)<\varepsilon\). If \(n>m\ge M\), then (1) gives \(|c_n-c_m|<\varepsilon\). The same conclusion holds when \(m>n\) by interchanging the indices, and when \(m=n\) the difference is zero. Thus \((c_n)\) is a Cauchy sequence. Completeness of the real numbers supplies a finite limit \(c\).

Finally, fix \(m\ge 0\) and let \(n\to\infty\) in the first inequality of (1). Since \(c_n\to c\) and absolute value is continuous,
\[
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
\]
This bounds the total remaining change after the first \(m\) corrections. The corrections may have either sign: the argument controls their absolute tails and requires no monotonicity. If \(A=0\), every correction is zero, so \(c=c_0\), as claimed. \(\square\)

Let \(A\ge 0\), let \(c_0\in\mathbb R\), and suppose the real corrections \(\delta_k\) satisfy
\[
|\delta_k|\le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)}
\qquad\text{for every integer }k\ge 0.
\]
Define the cumulative sensor value by
\[
c_n=c_0+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\delta_k,
\qquad n\ge 0,
\]
where the sum is empty when \(n=0\). We will show that \(c_n\) converges to a finite real limit \(c\), with
\[
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}
\qquad\text{for every integer }m\ge 0.
\]

For integers \(n>m\ge 0\), the difference \(c_n-c_m\) consists of the corrections added after \(c_m\). By the triangle inequality and the assumed bound,
\[
\begin{aligned}
|c_n-c_m|
&=\left|\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\delta_k\right|\\
&\le \sum_{k=m}^{n-1}|\delta_k|\\
&\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}\\
&=A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}
\left(\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}\right)\\
&=A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\\
&\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The sum telescopes because each negative term cancels the next positive term. Taking absolute values allows the corrections to have either sign, so no monotonicity is needed.

To establish convergence, let \(\varepsilon>0\) and choose an integer \(M\ge 0\) such that
\[
\frac{A}{M+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
For any distinct \(n,m\ge M\), apply the estimate with the larger index first to obtain
\[
|c_n-c_m|
\le \frac{A}{\min\{n,m\}+1}
\le \frac{A}{M+1}
<\varepsilon.
\]
When \(n=m\), the difference is zero. Thus \((c_n)\) is Cauchy, and completeness of \(\mathbb R\) gives a finite limit \(c\).

Finally, fix \(m\ge 0\). Letting \(n\to\infty\) in the sharper estimate and using continuity of absolute value gives
\[
|c-c_m|
=\lim_{n\to\infty}|c_n-c_m|
\le \lim_{n\to\infty}
A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)
=\frac{A}{m+1}.
\]
If \(A=0\), the assumption forces every correction to vanish, so \(c_n=c_0\) for all \(n\) and \(c=c_0\).

There are \(n\) labeled exhibit stations and \(n\) labeled tour groups, both numbered \(1,\ldots,n\). Each group visits exactly one station, and each station receives exactly one group. A box can be perfectly labeled and still have a small surprise waiting inside. This week's surprise was a bundle of blank envelopes, tied with the same string as the correspondence around it. The box had apparently decided that context deserved its own stationery.

We kept the envelopes. Their sizes match several letters in the bundle, and two carry faint impressions where a seal may once have pressed against them. That does not tell us which letter belonged in which envelope. It does give a future reader something to inspect, and it gives us a reason to describe the envelopes alongside the letters rather than treating them as packing material.

The catalogue note now says that the bundle includes eleven blank envelopes. It also records the impressions without identifying them as seals. We can see marks; their cause is less certain. A photograph would help someone decide whether to request the bundle, but the note is useful even before that photograph is made.

This is a small addition to the catalogue. Nobody has uncovered a lost correspondence or solved a mystery. We have simply made the contents a little easier to anticipate. If you request the bundle next week, the envelopes will still be there, kept flat in a separate sleeve within the same box. The string is there too, stored beside them. Some mornings, describing what we kept is most of the story.

A box can be perfectly labeled and still have a small surprise waiting inside. This week's surprise was a bundle of blank envelopes, tied with the same string as the correspondence around it. The box had apparently decided that context deserved its own stationery.

We kept the envelopes. Their sizes match several letters in the bundle, and two carry faint impressions where a seal may once have pressed against them. That does not tell us which letter belonged in which envelope. It does give a future reader something to inspect, and it gives us a reason to describe the envelopes alongside the letters rather than treating them as packing material.

The catalogue note now says that the bundle includes eleven blank envelopes. It also records the impressions without identifying them as seals. We can see marks; their cause is less certain. A photograph would help someone decide whether to request the bundle, but the note is useful even before that photograph is made.

This is a small addition to the catalogue. Nobody has uncovered a lost correspondence or solved a mystery. We have simply made the contents a little easier to anticipate. We found fewer flowering stems on the north slope during the second visit. The count fell from 34 to 19 within the marked strip. We counted stems rather than plants because several plants had more than one stem and we could not reliably trace them through the ground cover.

The strip was the same on both visits, but the conditions were not. On the first visit the grass had been recently cut. On the second it reached above some of the shorter stems. We therefore cannot tell how much of the difference reflects flowering and how much reflects visibility. Keeping the strip fixed controls where we looked; it does not ensure that we saw the same fraction of what was there.

The photographs show three stems that were flowering on the first visit and carried seed heads on the second. Those observations establish that at least some stems had changed stage. They do not account for the whole difference in the counts, and we have not assumed that every stem missing from the second count had set seed.

For the next visit, we will photograph the strip from the same two marked positions and record grass height at five fixed points. These additions will make the conditions easier to describe. They will not turn an unobserved stem into an observed one. The counts will remain useful as records of what we saw, provided that the change in visibility stays with them when they are summarized.

### Library entrance closure: Monday to Thursday

The library’s east entrance, facing the bus shelter, will be closed to everyone from Monday through Thursday while the pavement outside is replaced. The library will remain open on its usual schedule. The bus shelter will still be available, but the direct path from the shelter to the east entrance will be behind a temporary barrier.

Please use the west entrance, facing the playground. Visitors coming from the playground can use it as normal. If you are coming from the bus shelter, follow the signed path along the south side of the building to the west entrance. This route adds approximately 120 metres to the journey. It has no steps, but one section has a temporary firm mat over uneven ground.

During library opening hours, staff can meet visitors at the bus shelter and accompany them to the west entrance. If you would like assistance, call the library desk before setting out. You can also request assistance on arrival by calling the number displayed at the shelter, but a staff member may not be available immediately. The library cannot provide transport around the building.

The returns slot beside the east entrance will also be inaccessible. Books due Monday through Thursday, including books borrowed from another branch, may be returned on Friday without a late charge.

Heavy rain may delay the work. If the closure is extended, an updated notice will be posted at both entrances and at the bus shelter. The Friday return arrangement will remain in place unless that notice announces a further extension.

Welcome to the garden! Your assigned bed is marked with the number on your membership card. Some painted numbers have faded, so check the plan on the noticeboard if you are unsure. Please ask a steward before planting in a bed whose number you cannot read. The narrow strip beside the compost bins is planted collectively and is not an unclaimed bed.

The watering rota covers the collective strip and the young fruit trees. It does not cover individual beds, even if you have signed up for the rota. If you will be away, you can arrange separately for another gardener to water your bed. Add the arrangement to the noticeboard only with their agreement, so a request does not look like a job they have accepted.

Tools with blue handles are shared. Please return them to the shed before you leave, even if you plan to come back later that evening. Tools without blue handles may belong to another gardener, so do not assume they are shared. The shed code is on your membership card. Please close the door when you leave, as rain reaches the lower shelves when it is left open.

Weeds without seed heads can go in the green compost bay. Put weeds with seed heads in the covered brown bin. If you are unsure whether a plant has set seed, leave it in the brown bin and ask at the next steward session. This precaution helps us sort the compost and is no reflection on anyone’s gardening.

Stewards are usually here on Saturday mornings. Check the noticeboard for the next session and any cancellation. We are glad you are here, and we would much rather answer a small question before planting than help move a thriving crop out of somebody else’s bed.

We compared the current worksheet, which requires an operator to enter a blank reading separately for each sample, with a proposed worksheet that imports the blank from the instrument log. The proposed worksheet is intended to reduce transcription. We assessed agreement between the corrected values produced by the two worksheets and recorded the time required to produce them. The comparison did not assess accuracy against a known true concentration, as no certified reference material was included.

Twenty-four aliquots from eight prepared solutions, with three aliquots per solution, were measured in one session. Both worksheets processed the same instrument readings. Each aliquot was measured once, so the comparison contained no independent repeat measurements of an aliquot’s instrument signal. The manual worksheet was completed before the imported worksheet was generated, and the operator could not see the imported results during manual entry. Aliquots were measured in a fixed order by solution number.

In the initial comparison, corrected values agreed to the instrument’s displayed precision for 21 of the 24 aliquots. The three differences occurred in the final solution, where one blank entry had been copied into three rows of the manual worksheet. Inspection of the saved instrument log showed that this entry was 0.2 fluorescence units higher than the blank assigned to those rows in the log. Subtracting the higher blank made the three manual corrected values 0.2 units lower than the imported values.

After the initial comparison, we replaced the copied entry with the logged blank. The corrected values then agreed for all 24 aliquots at the displayed precision. This result is separate from the initial agreement of 21 of 24 values. It supports the conclusion that the import applied the intended subtraction to these inputs, but does not establish agreement at greater precision or correct blank assignment in future logs.

The initial differences are consistent with a transcription error in this session. Because a single copied entry affected three rows, the three discrepant aliquots do not establish three independent transcription errors. Nor can the observed error be used to estimate a routine operator error rate: only one operator completed the worksheet, and that operator knew the comparison concerned data entry.

The imported worksheet took four minutes to produce, compared with eleven minutes for manual entry and checking. These timings excluded instrument operation and the subsequent investigation of the discrepancy. They show a seven-minute saving in this session for this number of rows. Whether that saving persists when log formats change or an operator must resolve a missing blank was not measured.

The existing version returns keyboard focus to the same table cell after a note closes. Does speaking the row label help users find their place? This hypothetical study compared that version with a prototype that adds the spoken cue.

Twelve experienced screen-reader users completed four tasks with each version. Six used the cue version first, and six used the existing version first. The two task sets used different tables. Within each order group, the assignment of tables to versions was reversed for half the participants. We timed the interval from closing the note to activating the requested table entry. Time spent reading the note was outside that interval.

The median of the twelve participants’ mean completion times was 38 seconds with the cue and 41 seconds without it. The three-second difference is between those two medians, not the median of the twelve within-person differences. Seven participants had a lower mean time with the cue, three had a higher mean, and two had equal means at the recorded precision. We have not calculated a confidence interval or performed a significance test.

The interviews suggest an orientation benefit for some users, but they also identify a problem with the added speech. Nine participants said the cue helped them feel oriented. Four of those nine also recalled occasions when it interrupted speech they were still listening to. These reports describe participants’ experience, rather than a measured improvement in orientation. The remaining three participants did not report an orientation benefit. None asked for the feature to be removed from the prototype, but we did not ask anyone to choose a default. That leaves the default setting undecided.

The task order reduced the alignment between version and practice without ruling out learning effects. Some participants may have learned a search strategy in the first set and carried it into the second. The findings also have a limited scope: we recruited experienced users, and the prototype’s tables were short enough to fit on one screen. We do not know how less experienced users would respond or how the cue would affect performance on large tables.

For the product team, the cue is worth further investigation because some participants reported that it helped them regain their place. The waiting list has grown, and the proposal to divide every returning gardener’s bed in half responds to a real concern. There are twenty full beds and ten households waiting, and membership should not depend on being lucky enough to have joined years ago. But access to land also includes the chance to keep a crop through its growing cycle. I support dividing vacant beds first because it would admit more households while giving returning gardeners one more season before their beds might change.

Four full beds will become vacant at the end of this season. Dividing them would create eight half beds. If every offer is accepted, eight households would receive a bed and two would remain on the waiting list. That is a substantial increase in access, but it does not clear the list. The reason to choose this approach is that we can make those eight offers without requiring every returning gardener to remove established planting at once.

The objection that established planting can preserve an established advantage deserves an answer. Planting a perennial cannot give someone a permanent claim to shared land. Our membership agreement promises a bed for a season, with renewal decided annually. Under my proposal, returning gardeners would keep their present beds for one more season, and the committee would publish the following season’s allocation rule before renewals open. The extra season would allow a transition without creating a new entitlement.

That published rule should cover both returning and new members. A household accepting a half bed also needs notice if its bed might later be merged or moved. Otherwise, we would give new members the same uncertainty we are trying to address for current gardeners. I do not yet have a preferred permanent bed size. We can decide how to handle this transition while leaving that question open, provided we commit to announcing the next rule before households make their renewal decisions.

The raised beds require separate consideration. Two of the twenty full beds are reserved for gardeners who need them, and neither is among the four becoming vacant. My proposal keeps that reservation and the existing access assessment unchanged. A standard half bed is not automatically a substitute for a raised bed simply because we can compare their areas on a plan.

Starting with vacancies also has a practical drawback: the four vacant beds are at the far end of the site, so all eight new households would begin in the same area. We could invite returning members to exchange locations voluntarily, but we cannot count on those exchanges. Nor should a new household have to negotiate a private favor to obtain a usable route to its bed. Before making offers, the committee should check the paths to the new half beds and report any access problem it cannot resolve. Voluntary exchanges may help with the concentration of new members, but they do not remove the committee’s responsibility to address access.

For these offers, the waiting list would retain its current order. This preserves whatever disadvantages people faced in learning about the list, and keeping the order does not resolve that concern. But changing it during this allocation would introduce another contested decision without giving households notice. We can begin reviewing how the list is advertised now. Any future change to its ordering should be announced before it applies.

I would like the next set of fraction worksheets to include one worked example followed by a problem in which pupils explain a different method. At present, every example ends with a sequence of steps, and every practice problem asks pupils to repeat it. This is efficient when the aim is to practise the sequence, but I am less sure it tells us whether pupils understand why it applies.

During last week’s lesson, several pupils added the numerators and denominators separately after copying an example that used equal denominators. I had not collected a starting question, so I do not know how many already had this misunderstanding. Nor can I tell whether the worked example caused it or simply exposed it. What I did see was that pupils could copy correctly on the first practice question and still show the misunderstanding on the next. That gives me a reason to ask for an explanation as well as a calculation.

The proposed problem would show two correct solutions to the same addition, one using equivalent fractions and one using a diagram. Pupils would explain where the same quantity appears in both. This would give us something to consider beyond whether they can repeat the steps. I would avoid asking which method is always better: a diagram may be illuminating for these numbers and cumbersome for others. I would not want a useful representation to become another compulsory routine.

The explanation problem will take space and lesson time, so I would replace one repetition question rather than add an extra page. Pupils who still need practice with the original sequence could use the spare practice sheet we already have. That makes room for the change, though it does not show that one explanation problem will meet everyone’s needs.

We could try the revised sheet in one lesson and collect the explanation responses before deciding whether to keep it. We would be looking at what pupils’ responses reveal and what teachers find workable. Without a comparison planned in advance, the trial would not establish whether the sheet improves attainment. I think the chance to learn more about pupils’ understanding, while finding out whether the task fits into a lesson, is enough reason to try this limited change.

**Claim.** Let \((a_n)_{n\geq 1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing real sequence with limit zero, and put
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then every \(d_n\) is nonnegative, and
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=a_1.
\]
For every integer \(N\geq 1\), the tail after \(N\) terms is
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is an \(N\) such that this tail is less than \(\varepsilon\).

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\geq a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\geq 0\).

To establish convergence, we examine the partial sum of the first \(N\) terms. Substituting the definition of \(d_n\), we get
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_N=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
&=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\
&=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each intermediate term cancels, leaving only the first and last terms. Thus
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Because \(a_n\to 0\), this difference tends to zero. Hence the partial sums tend to \(a_1\), which is precisely what it means for the series to converge to \(a_1\).

Now fix \(N\geq 1\). For every integer \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_{N,M}=\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
&=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular,
\[
|T_{N,M}-a_{N+1}|=a_{M+1}\longrightarrow 0
\qquad\text{as }M\to\infty.
\]
The infinite tail is the limit of these finite sums, so
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]

Finally, given \(\varepsilon>0\), the assumption \(a_n\to 0\) provides an integer \(K\geq 1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) whenever \(k\geq K\). Taking \(N=K\), we obtain
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]

No strict decrease was needed: equal consecutive terms simply give \(d_n=0\). If \(a_1=0\), nonnegativity and monotonicity force every \(a_n\) to be zero, and the same identities apply. \(\square\)

To find the sum of the series, consider its partial sums. The intermediate terms cancel:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_N
&=\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n\\
&=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\
&=a_1-a_{N+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the distance from \(S_N\) to \(a_1\) is exactly
\[
|S_N-a_1|=a_{N+1}.
\]
Because \(a_n\to 0\), this distance tends to zero. By definition, a series converges when its partial sums have a limit, so
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n=\lim_{N\to\infty}S_N=a_1.
\]

Now fix \(N\ge 1\). For every integer \(M>N\), the same cancellation gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
&=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The difference between this finite sum and \(a_{N+1}\) has absolute value \(a_{M+1}\), which tends to zero as \(M\to\infty\). Therefore the tail series converges, with
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]

Finally, let \(\varepsilon>0\). Since \(a_n\to 0\), there is an integer \(K\ge 1\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) whenever \(k\ge K\). For every \(N\ge K\), we have \(N+1\ge K\), and hence
\[
0\le \sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n
=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
All the identities remain valid when consecutive terms are equal, including the case in which every term is zero. \(\square\)

**Claim.** Let \((a_n)_{n\ge 1}\) be a nonnegative, nonincreasing real sequence with limit \(0\), and define
\[
d_n=a_n-a_{n+1}.
\]
Then \(d_n\ge 0\) for every \(n\), the series \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}d_n\) converges to \(a_1\), and for every integer \(N\ge 1\),
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}.
\]
In particular, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the tail after \(N\) terms is less than \(\varepsilon\) for some \(N\).

**Proof.** Since the sequence is nonincreasing, \(a_n\ge a_{n+1}\), so \(d_n\ge0\). For integers \(M>N\ge1\), the finite sums telescope:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n
&=(a_1-a_2)+(a_2-a_3)+\cdots+(a_N-a_{N+1})\\
&=a_1-a_{N+1},
\end{aligned}
\]
and
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=N+1}^{M}d_n
&=(a_{N+1}-a_{N+2})+\cdots+(a_M-a_{M+1})\\
&=a_{N+1}-a_{M+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

As \(N\) increases, \(a_{N+1}\to0\), so the first identity shows that the partial sums \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}d_n\) approach \(a_1\). This is exactly convergence of the series to \(a_1\).

Now fix \(N\). As \(M\) increases, \(a_{M+1}\to0\), so the second identity shows that the sums from \(n=N+1\) to \(M\) approach \(a_{N+1}\). Thus the tail after the first \(N\) terms is \(a_{N+1}\).

Finally, since \(a_n\to0\), for any \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an integer \(K\) such that \(a_k<\varepsilon\) whenever \(k\ge K\). Choose \(N=\max(1,K)\). Then \(N+1\ge K\), and the tail is
\[
\sum_{n=N+1}^{\infty}d_n=a_{N+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
The argument also covers \(a_1=0\) and equal consecutive terms: no strict decrease is needed.

**Claim.** Arrange \(n\ge 3\) labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) be the number of \(k\)-element selections with no two neighboring plots selected, including the pair that meets across the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

**Proof.** If \(k=0\), the empty selection is the only selection. The formula agrees:
\[
\frac{n}{n-0}\binom{n}{0}=1.
\]

Now suppose \(k\ge 1\). We count valid selections with one selected plot marked as the start. Each valid selection has exactly \(k\) choices for this mark, so the number of marked selections is
\[
kA(n,k).
\]

We can also construct a marked selection by choosing its start and the gaps between its selected plots. There are \(n\) choices for the start. Beginning there, number the selected plots \(1,\ldots,k\) in clockwise order, and let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between selected plot \(i\) and the next selected plot. The final gap \(g_k\) leads back to the start, so it includes the circular boundary. When \(k=1\), this single gap contains all \(n-1\) other plots.

The condition that no selected plots are neighbors says that every gap is positive. Since the gaps contain all the unselected plots, we have
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k,
\qquad g_i\ge 1.
\]

To count these ordered gap tuples, place \(n-k\) objects in a row. Choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) spaces between consecutive objects and insert separators there. The resulting \(k\) nonempty groups have sizes \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\). Conversely, each positive gap tuple determines exactly these separator positions. Thus there are
\[
\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
\]
gap tuples. For \(k=1\), we choose no separators, giving the one tuple \((n-1)\).

A chosen start and gap tuple determine exactly one marked selection: select the start, leave the next \(g_1\) plots unselected, select the next plot, and continue clockwise. The \(k\) selected plots and the gaps use
\[
k+(g_1+\cdots+g_k)=n
\]
plots, so the construction returns to the start after one full circuit. All gaps are positive, including the final one, so the selection is valid. Conversely, every marked selection gives exactly one start and gap tuple. Therefore,
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}.
\]

Dividing by \(k\) is legitimate because each unmarked selection was counted exactly once for each of its \(k\) possible marks. Since \(k\ge 1\), we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(n,k)
&=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\\
&=\frac{n}{k}\,
  \frac{(n-k-1)!}{(k-1)!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\,
  \frac{(n-k)!}{k!(n-2k)!}\\
&=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(n-2k\ge 0\), and \(n-k>0\), by the assumed range of \(k\).

If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), the positive gaps sum to \(k\), so every gap is exactly one. These selections are included in the argument. We do not divide by rotations: the plots have distinct fixed labels, and the division by \(k\) removes only the choice of a marked start. \(\square\)

&=\frac{n}{k}\,

If \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap is one, which the construction allows. We do not divide by rotations: the plots have distinct fixed labels, and rotating a selection may select different labeled plots. \(\square\)

Claim. Arrange \(n\ge 3\) labeled garden plots in a circle. For an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\), let \(A(n,k)\) be the number of \(k\)-element selections with no two neighboring plots selected, including the pair that meets across the circular boundary. Then
\[
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]

Proof. If \(k=0\), the only selection is the empty one, so \(A(n,0)=1\). The formula also gives \(1\).

Now assume \(k\ge 1\). Count pairs consisting of a valid selection and one of its selected plots marked as the start. Each selection has \(k\) plots that can be marked, so there are \(kA(n,k)\) such pairs.

To count the same pairs another way, choose the start plot in \(n\) ways. Moving clockwise from it, let \(g_i\) be the number of unselected plots between the \(i\)th selected plot and the next selected plot, for \(i=1,\ldots,k\). When \(k=1\), this gap consists of all the other plots before returning to the start. The selection is valid exactly when every \(g_i\ge 1\), and the gaps contain all \(n-k\) unselected plots. Thus
\[
g_1+\cdots+g_k=n-k.
\]

The number of ordered \(k\)-tuples of positive integers with this sum is \(\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\): arrange \(n-k\) objects in a row and choose \(k-1\) of the \(n-k-1\) spaces between them as separators. The numbers of objects in the resulting \(k\) groups are the gaps. This counts the marked selections because a start plot and its ordered gaps determine exactly one selection, and each marked selection gives exactly one such choice.

There are therefore \(n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}\) marked selections. Equating the two counts gives
\[
kA(n,k)=n\binom{n-k-1}{k-1},
\qquad
A(n,k)=\frac{n}{k}\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}
=\frac{n}{n-k}\binom{n-k}{k}.
\]
The last equality follows by expanding the binomial coefficients.

When \(n\) is even and \(k=n/2\), every gap is one, which is allowed. The division by \(k\) is legitimate because each selection has exactly \(k\) choices of marked plot, and \(k\ge1\) in this part of the proof. The labels stay fixed throughout, so no quotient by rotations is involved.

The compost thermometer has returned from its brief career as a dibber. It is back on the hook inside the shed, where it can resume measuring temperature rather than making holes. Please use the wooden dibbers for planting. They have fewer opinions about heat.

This month we are comparing the middle of the active heap with its outer edge. On your rota day, take one reading at each marked position and record both on the sheet. Push the probe to the mark on its shaft, wait until the display settles, and wipe it before returning it to the hook. If the display never settles, write that down instead of choosing the number you like best.

A warmer middle is interesting, but a single pair of readings will not tell us whether the whole heap is ready to use. We are collecting observations over the month. The stewards will also inspect the material before deciding whether to open the bay for collection. Until the notice changes, please keep adding suitable material to the active bay and leave the resting bay alone.

The recording sheet has room for comments because weather, recently added material, and an uncooperative display may help explain a reading. You do not need to write a small novel. “Heavy rain this morning” is useful. “The heap has entered a troubled period” is less useful, though we appreciate the concern.

The balance readings were stable during the twenty-minute observation period. Stability here means that the displayed mass stayed within 0.01 grams of its initial displayed value. It does not mean that the initial value was accurate. We did not place a certified reference mass on the balance during this check.

The same sealed container remained on the pan throughout. This avoids variability from replacing the container, but it also means that the check says nothing about repeatability after unloading and reloading. The maintenance record should preserve this distinction.

The room temperature recorded at the start and end was the same to the wall sensor's displayed precision. There were no readings between those times. We therefore cannot exclude a temporary temperature change during the observation period, nor can we determine whether such a change would have affected this balance. The temperature record is context for the check, not a correction applied to the mass readings.

No visible condensation appeared on the container. That observation does not measure moisture exchange, because the check included neither a humidity measurement nor an independent mass reference. We report it to describe what the operator saw, not to establish a mechanism for the stable display.

These results support a narrow entry in the maintenance log: no displayed drift beyond the stated tolerance during this placement and observation period. A calibration decision would require the separate reference-mass procedure.

The amber indicator on the curing-line monitor appeared just after washdown on three of the last five morning shifts. It means the humidity probe’s reading is outside the range accepted by the controller, but it does not tell us whether the room is too humid or the probe’s reading is unreliable. Rain may change what a recorder detects as well as how often animals call. Before interpreting differences between wet and dry surveys, we therefore need to understand how rain affects the recordings. This pilot examined whether a rain shield changes the output of one fixed call detector. It did not estimate animal abundance. Calling activity itself may be an ecological quantity of interest, depending on the question.

We placed two recorders in each of twelve habitat patches, one shielded and one exposed, with shielded and exposed positions assigned by a coin toss within each patch. The devices recorded simultaneously. We analyzed twelve paired ten-minute windows per patch, giving 144 paired windows. Field logs classified 48 windows as wet and 96 as dry. Weather was not assigned. A window was positive when the detector marked at least one target call, using the same detector settings throughout.

During wet windows, the devices agreed in 29 of 48 pairs. The shielded device alone was positive in twelve pairs, and the exposed device alone in seven. During dry windows, the devices agreed in 84 of 96 pairs, with five shield-only positives and seven exposed-only positives. Agreement includes both pairs in which both devices were positive and pairs in which neither was positive. Because this summary does not separate those outcomes, the agreement counts cannot be interpreted as the number of windows containing calls.

The direction of discordance differed between the observed weather categories: shield-only positives were more frequent than exposed-only positives in wet windows, while exposed-only positives were slightly more frequent in dry windows. The wet-window pattern is consistent with shielding changing detector output under rain. Without independent call labeling, however, we cannot determine whether the additional positives were genuine calls. Nor does the comparison establish that rain reduced calling. Weather was observed rather than assigned, and repeated windows within patches mean that the 144 paired windows are not 144 independent ecological replicates.

The paired recordings show disagreement between shielded and exposed detector outputs and identify a measurement question to resolve before using these recordings to assess ecological trends. A future study could use blinded human labeling to assess whether detections correspond to genuine calls and include more patches to increase ecological replication. That study has not been run. The present results describe the direction of discordance within the observed weather categories, while leaving its biological interpretation unresolved.
