We introduced the persistence rule because a single pressure spike need not indicate a valve fault. It raises an alarm after two threshold crossings within a cycle. The comparison rule uses a higher threshold and raises an alarm after one crossing. Both thresholds and the persistence requirement were fixed using a separate setup recording, without using the evaluation recordings. Because the rules differ in both threshold and persistence requirement, the comparison evaluates their combined effect rather than isolating the effect of persistence.

The held-out bench set contains 120 cycles from one machine: 30 with an induced valve fault and 90 with no induced fault. Each rule produces at most one alarm per cycle. The persistence rule alarmed in 24 of the 30 fault cycles and eight of the 90 no-fault cycles. The comparison rule alarmed in 21 fault cycles and three no-fault cycles. The persistence rule therefore detected more induced faults in this set, at the cost of alarming in more no-fault cycles. Here, “no-fault” means that no fault was induced. We did not dismantle the machine after every cycle to exclude every possible defect.

To compare alarm delays on the same cycles, we used the 18 fault cycles that triggered both rules. On these cycles, the mean time from the logged fault onset to the first alarm was 2.1 seconds for the persistence rule and 2.8 seconds for the comparison rule. This comparison excludes faults detected by only one rule and faults missed by both, so the shorter mean delay applies only to the shared detections.

Although transient spikes motivated the persistence requirement, the observed benefit was higher detection of induced faults, accompanied by more alarms in no-fault cycles. The lower threshold changes which cycles can trigger an alarm, and combining it with a persistence requirement does not by itself establish better false-alarm control.

These recordings compare two fixed rules under one bench arrangement. They do not establish performance on a production line or with naturally developing faults. We have not selected a preferred rule: that choice depends on the relative costs of missing a fault and interrupting a cycle, which were not measured.

The committee should choose the handling replica for the navigation exhibit this season. The exhibit asks visitors to work out how a reading changes when an instrument is tilted. Visitors can tilt the replica, but they would not be permitted to tilt the original. The replica therefore fits the activity we have designed, though we still need to test whether that activity helps visitors understand the question.

The original’s availability on loan is an opportunity that may not recur. It also offers something the replica cannot: a material connection to the instrument’s working history. A maker’s correction remains visible on its scale, a detail that could support an account of repair and adaptation. A photograph would not give every visitor the same experience as standing beside the object. These are reasons to consider an exhibit centered on the original’s history. Our current text, however, concerns reading and error. Making repair central would require a redesign and a different use of the season’s remaining preparation time.

Cost supports choosing the replica, but it does not rule out the loan. The quoted loan cost is 18,000 units from the exhibit budget, including transport, insurance, and a sealed case. The replica would cost 7,000 units, including replacement parts for the season. Neither quote is a complete estimate of staff time, and both options fit the allocated budget. The main reason to prefer the replica is what visitors would be able to do with it. Its lower quoted cost would also leave resources for testing the activity.

That testing remains necessary. The replica’s moving parts could distract visitors from the question, or visitors could turn them without noticing the scale. A visitor trial has not yet happened, so we cannot claim that handling has improved understanding. Choosing the replica would give us an object suited to the planned activity and resources to investigate whether the activity works.

We should proceed with the replica, trial the activity with visitors, and retain a clearly labeled photograph of the original with an explanation of why the replica can be handled. If the committee instead wants the original’s history to become the exhibit’s central question, it should explicitly authorize that change in direction.

We propose revising the short discovery labels attached to twenty digitized collections. Some labels repeat terms from old inventory headings without explaining whose categories they were. These labels help readers decide which collection to open, but they also communicate how the archive describes the collection today. Revising them would change that description. The scanned inventories would remain available exactly as they are.

The existing labels offer a real retrieval benefit: a reader following a quotation from an inventory can recognize the same words in the catalogue. A reader who has not seen the inventory, however, may understand those words as the archive’s present description. Repeating an old heading therefore serves readers arriving through historical quotations while potentially misleading readers encountering the collection for the first time. The proposal needs to account for both.

We propose using a current descriptive label, adding a note that identifies the original heading, and retaining that heading as a searchable alternative. The quoted words would remain a way to find the collection without standing alone as its present description. Search results would show the current label, and the note would be visible when a reader opens the record. This changes how the archive introduces the collection, while leaving the words in the historical document and the document itself available.

A replacement label necessarily interprets the collection. So does choosing an inventory heading as the main label, even when that choice appears simply to reproduce existing text. Recognizing that both choices involve interpretation does not make every replacement equally good. A new label should describe the contents at the level the collection supports, and the note should make its relationship to the old wording clear. We have drafted labels for the twenty collections, but readers and subject specialists have not yet reviewed them.

There is also a practical objection: adding notes can make a short catalogue harder to scan. Keeping the note inside the record preserves the brevity of search results, but it means readers scanning those results may not immediately see the historical wording. The proposed arrangement thus preserves the old heading as a search term at the cost of making it less immediately visible. It does not fully resolve the competing needs.

These limits support a trial with the twenty collections, followed by checks of both successful and failed searches. We have no evidence yet that the change will improve retrieval. The trial would test whether this arrangement can provide context while preserving a route from historical quotations. Expansion should wait until those checks give us a basis for judging how well it serves both purposes.

These tradeoffs support a limited trial with the twenty collections, followed by checks of both successful and failed searches. We have no evidence yet that the changes will improve retrieval. The trial would test whether this approach can provide context while preserving a route from historical quotations. Expanding the policy before those checks would go beyond the present case for it.

We propose revising the short discovery labels for twenty digitized collections. Some labels repeat terms from old inventory headings without explaining whose categories they reflect. The scanned inventories would remain unchanged and available. The revision would affect the text that helps readers decide which collection to open. Because that text also shapes how the archive represents a collection, it is more than packaging.

Keeping the existing labels has a retrieval benefit: readers following a quotation from an inventory can find the same words in the catalogue. But readers who have not seen the inventory may take those words as the archive’s current description. Repeating an old heading can therefore help readers follow one route into the material while misleading readers who arrive another way.

We propose a current descriptive label, a note identifying the original heading, and the original heading retained as a searchable alternative. This keeps the quoted words as a route to the collection without making them stand alone as its present description. The original wording would remain in the historical document, and the old inventory would remain available. Search results would show the current label; readers would see the note when they open the record.

Any replacement label interprets the collection. The same is true when an inventory heading is chosen as the main label, even if that choice looks like copying. Since interpretation is unavoidable, the question is which label best describes the collection. A new label should describe the contents only as specifically as the collection supports, and the note should show its relationship to the old wording. We have drafted labels for the twenty collections, but readers and subject specialists have not reviewed them.

Notes may make a short catalogue harder to scan. Keeping the note inside the record addresses that concern, but means readers scanning search results may not see the historical wording immediately. The proposal therefore balances the need for context against the convenience of seeing that wording in search results.

We recommend a limited trial with the twenty collections, followed by checks of successful and failed searches. We do not yet know whether the trial will improve retrieval. It will test whether this approach provides context while preserving a route from historical quotations. Expanding the policy before those checks would go beyond the evidence for the present proposal.

Let \(A\ge 0\), let \(c_0\in\mathbb R\), and suppose the real corrections \(\delta_k\) satisfy
\[
|\delta_k|\le \frac{A}{(k+1)(k+2)}
\qquad(k\ge 0).
\]
Define the cumulative corrected value by
\[
c_n=c_0+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\delta_k
\qquad(n\ge 0),
\]
where the sum is empty when \(n=0\). We show that \(c_n\) converges to a finite real limit \(c\), with
\[
|c-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}
\qquad(m\ge 0).
\]

For integers \(n>m\ge 0\), the difference \(c_n-c_m\) consists of the corrections from index \(m\) through \(n-1\). By the triangle inequality and the assumed bound,
\[
\begin{aligned}
|c_n-c_m|
&=\left|\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\delta_k\right|\\
&\le \sum_{k=m}^{n-1}|\delta_k|\\
&\le A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}\frac{1}{(k+1)(k+2)}\\
&=A\sum_{k=m}^{n-1}
\left(\frac{1}{k+1}-\frac{1}{k+2}\right)\\
&=A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\\
&\le \frac{A}{m+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The penultimate equality follows because the intermediate terms cancel.

This estimate makes all sufficiently late cumulative values close to one another. Indeed, given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose an integer \(M\ge 0\) such that
\[
\frac{A}{M+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
For any \(n,m\ge M\) with \(n>m\), we have
\[
|c_n-c_m|\le \frac{A}{m+1}
\le \frac{A}{M+1}<\varepsilon.
\]
The same bound holds when \(m>n\) by interchanging the indices, and the difference is zero when \(m=n\). Thus \((c_n)\) is Cauchy. Completeness of \(\mathbb R\) gives a finite limit \(c\).

To bound the remaining correction after index \(m-1\), fix \(m\ge 0\) and let \(n\to\infty\) in the sharper estimate above. Since \(c_n\to c\) and absolute value is continuous,
\[
\begin{aligned}
|c-c_m|
&=\lim_{n\to\infty}|c_n-c_m|\\
&\le \lim_{n\to\infty}
A\left(\frac{1}{m+1}-\frac{1}{n+1}\right)\\
&=\frac{A}{m+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The corrections may have either sign: the argument bounds their absolute values and requires no monotonicity of the corrections or cumulative values. If \(A=0\), every correction is zero, so \(c_n=c=c_0\).

There are \(n\) labeled exhibit stations and \(n\) labeled tour groups, both indexed by \(1,\ldots,n\). Each group visits exactly one station, and each station receives exactly one group. Thus a schedule is a permutation \(\pi\), where group \(i\) visits station \(\pi(i)\). A schedule is **clear** if
\[
\pi(i)\ne i \qquad \text{for every }i.
\]
The matching labels designate pairings to avoid. They do not describe physical positions, and the stations need not be arranged in a line or a circle.

For every integer \(n\ge 0\), the number \(D_n\) of clear schedules is
\[
D_n
=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!
=n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.
\]
We use \(0!=1\) and include the unique empty schedule when \(n=0\).

To prove the formula, we assign each schedule a weight that is \(1\) when the schedule is clear and \(0\) otherwise. For a fixed schedule \(\pi\), let
\[
F(\pi)=\{i:\pi(i)=i\}
\]
be the set of labels whose pairings we wanted to avoid. Consider the weight
\[
w(\pi)=\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}.
\]
If \(F(\pi)\) is empty, its only subset is the empty set, so this sum has one term and equals \(1\). If \(F(\pi)\) is nonempty, choose a label \(j\in F(\pi)\). Every subset that does not contain \(j\) pairs with the subset obtained by adding \(j\). Their contributions cancel because
\[
(-1)^{|S|}+(-1)^{|S|+1}=0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
w(\pi)=
\begin{cases}
1,&\text{if }\pi\text{ is clear},\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Summing these weights over all schedules therefore counts exactly the clear schedules. We can then regroup the finite sum by the subset \(S\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_n
&=\sum_{\pi}\sum_{S\subseteq F(\pi)}(-1)^{|S|}\\
&=\sum_{S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}}(-1)^{|S|}
   \#\{\pi:S\subseteq F(\pi)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The regrouping counts the same pairs \((\pi,S)\) in a different order: first choose \(S\), then count all schedules that fix every label in \(S\).

Suppose \(S\) has \(k\) members. Requiring \(\pi(i)=i\) for every \(i\in S\) assigns those \(k\) groups to their matching stations. The remaining \(n-k\) groups must be assigned bijectively to the remaining \(n-k\) stations, giving
\[
\#\{\pi:S\subseteq F(\pi)\}=(n-k)!.
\]
These schedules may also fix labels outside \(S\). We are requiring every label in \(S\) to be fixed, not requiring \(S\) to be the full set of fixed labels. The cancellation above accounts for those additional fixed labels.

There are \(\binom{n}{k}\) subsets \(S\) of size \(k\), so grouping by size gives
\[
D_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}(-1)^k\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!.
\]
Finally,
\[
\binom{n}{k}(n-k)!
=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}(n-k)!
=\frac{n!}{k!},
\]
which yields
\[
D_n=n!\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}.
\]

When \(n=0\), the empty schedule has no forbidden pairings, and the formula gives \(D_0=1\). When \(n=1\), the only schedule assigns group \(1\) to station \(1\), so \(D_1=0\). When \(n=2\), the sole clear schedule swaps the assignments: group \(1\) visits station \(2\), and group \(2\) visits station \(1\).

A box can be perfectly labeled and still have a small surprise waiting inside. This week's surprise was a bundle of blank envelopes, tied with the same string as the correspondence around it. The box had apparently decided that context deserved its own stationery.

We kept the envelopes. Their sizes match several letters in the bundle, and two carry faint impressions where a seal may once have pressed against them. That does not tell us which letter belonged in which envelope. It does give a future reader something to inspect, and it gives us a reason to describe the envelopes alongside the letters rather than treating them as packing material.

The catalogue note now says that the bundle includes eleven blank envelopes. It also records the impressions without identifying them as seals. We can see marks; their cause is less certain. A photograph would help someone decide whether to request the bundle, but the note is useful even before that photograph is made.

This is a small addition to the catalogue. Nobody has uncovered a lost correspondence or solved a mystery. We have simply made the contents a little easier to anticipate. If you request the bundle next week, the envelopes will still be there, kept flat in a separate sleeve within the same box. The string is there too, stored beside them. Some mornings, describing what we kept is most of the story.

We kept the envelopes. Their sizes match several letters in the bundle, and two carry faint impressions where a seal may once have pressed against them. It does give a future reader something to inspect, and it gives us a reason to describe the envelopes alongside the letters rather than treating them as packing material.

We found fewer flowering stems on the north slope during the second visit. The count fell from 34 to 19 within the marked strip. We counted stems rather than plants because several plants had more than one stem and we could not reliably trace them through the ground cover.

The strip was the same on both visits, but the conditions were not. On the first visit the grass had been recently cut. On the second it reached above some of the shorter stems. We therefore cannot tell how much of the difference reflects flowering and how much reflects visibility. Keeping the strip fixed controls where we looked, but it does not ensure that we saw the same fraction of what was there.

The photographs show three stems that were flowering on the first visit and carried seed heads on the second. Those observations establish that at least some stems had changed stage. They do not account for the whole difference in the counts, and we have not assumed that every stem missing from the second count had set seed.

For the next visit, we will photograph the strip from the same two marked positions and record grass height at five fixed points. These additions will help us describe the conditions, but they will not account for stems we did not see. The counts will remain useful as records of what we saw, provided that summaries also describe the change in visibility.
